claim: Most proteins in the fecal fluid of Acromyrmex leaf-cutting ants function as biomass degrading enzymes.
source: Here we present a full proteome of the fecal fluid of Acromyrmex leaf-cutting ants, showing that most proteins function as biomass degrading enzymes
evidence: The proteome analysis identified proteins and their functions, showing the majority are biomass degrading enzymes.

claim: Approximately 85% of fecal fluid proteins are produced by the fungus and ingested, but not digested, by the ants.
source: Here we present a full proteome of the fecal fluid of Acromyrmex leaf-cutting ants, showing that most proteins function as biomass degrading enzymes and that ca. 85% are produced by the fungus and ingested, but not digested, by the ants.
evidence: The proteome analysis determined the origin of proteins, showing 86 of 101 core proteins originated from the fungal symbiont.

claim: Hydrogen peroxide producing oxidoreductases were remarkably common in the fecal fluid proteome.
source: Hydrogen peroxide producing oxidoreductases were remarkably common in the proteome
evidence: The proteome analysis identified multiple oxidoreductases in the fecal fluid.

claim: Fenton reactions take place in special substrate pellets to degrade plant cell wall polymers.
source: Our biochemical assays confirmed that these so-called Fenton reactions do indeed take place in special substrate pellets, presumably to degrade plant cell wall polymers.
evidence: Biochemical assays confirmed the presence of Fenton reaction components and hydroxyl radical production.

claim: The symbiotic partnership manages a combination of oxidative and enzymatic biomass degradation.
source: This implies that the symbiotic partnership manages a combination of oxidative and enzymatic biomass degradation, an achievement that surpasses current human bioconversion technology.
evidence: The proteome and biochemical assays show both enzymatic and oxidative (Fenton) degradation mechanisms.

claim: The symbiotic biomass degradation achievement surpasses current human bioconversion technology.
source: This implies that the symbiotic partnership manages a combination of oxidative and enzymatic biomass degradation, an achievement that surpasses current human bioconversion technology.
evidence: This is a comparative claim based on the authors' interpretation of the findings relative to known human technology.

claim: Leaf-cutting ants belong to the genera Acromyrmex and Atta and form the phylogenetic crown group of the attine fungus-growing ants.
source: The leaf-cutting ants belong to the genera Acromyrmex and Atta and form the phylogenetic crown group of the attine fungus-growing ants, which all live in mutualistic symbiosis with fungus-garden symbionts (Mueller et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mueller et al., 2005.

claim: All attine ants live in mutualistic symbiosis with fungus-garden symbionts.
source: The leaf-cutting ants belong to the genera Acromyrmex and Atta and form the phylogenetic crown group of the attine fungus-growing ants, which all live in mutualistic symbiosis with fungus-garden symbionts (Mueller et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mueller et al., 2005.

claim: Basal branches of the attine clade farm a considerable diversity of mostly leucocoprinaceous fungi, normally in underground chambers.
source: While the basal branches of the attine clade farm a considerable diversity of mostly leucocoprinaceous fungi, normally in underground chambers (Branstetter et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Branstetter et al., 2017.

claim: Leaf-cutting ants almost exclusively farm what has been described as the highly variable cultivar species Leucocoprinus gongylophorus.
source: the leaf-cutting ants almost exclusively farm what has been described as the highly variable cultivar species Leucocoprinus gongylophorus (Schultz and Brady, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schultz and Brady, 2008.

claim: Ants cut leaf fragments from the canopy and understory and bring them back to their nest to be processed as growth substrate for the cultivar.
source: The ants cut leaf fragments from the canopy and understory and bring them back to their nest to be processed as growth substrate for the cultivar.
evidence: This is established knowledge about leaf-cutting ant behavior.

claim: Processing of leaf fragments involves chewing forage material into smaller pieces, which are mixed with fecal fluid and deposited as new substrate on the actively growing parts of the garden.
source: This involves chewing forage material into smaller pieces, which are mixed with fecal fluid and deposited as new substrate on the actively growing parts of the garden (Weber, 1966).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Weber, 1966.

claim: The deep ancestors of the attine ants and their fungal cultivars were hunter-gatherers and saprotrophs, respectively.
source: The deep ancestors of the attine ants and their fungal cultivars were hunter-gatherers and saprotrophs (Schultz and Brady, 2008), respectively
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schultz and Brady, 2008.

claim: Neither ancestral attine ants nor their fungal cultivars were adapted for efficiently degrading fresh plant material.
source: which implies that none of them were adapted for efficiently degrading fresh plant material.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ancestral lifestyles of the organisms.

claim: All phylogenetically basal attine ants provision their gardens with dead plant debris.
source: Neither was there any need initially, because all phylogenetically basal attine ants provision their gardens with dead plant debris.
evidence: This is established knowledge about basal attine ant behavior.

claim: There is a striking difference between the small colonies of basal attine ants and the large colonies of leaf-cutting ants which are conspicuous functional herbivores with a large ecological footprint.
source: There is a striking difference between the small colonies of these basal attine ants and the large colonies of leaf-cutting ants which are conspicuous functional herbivores with a large ecological footprint (Mehdiabadi and Schultz, 2010; Mueller, 2002; Shik et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mehdiabadi and Schultz, 2010; Mueller, 2002; Shik et al., 2021.

claim: Most leaves that ants harvest are heavily protected against herbivory by recalcitrant cell walls and toxic substances.
source: However, most of the leaves that the ants harvest are heavily protected against herbivory by recalcitrant cell walls and toxic substances (Chen, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen, 2008.

claim: The 'higher' attine ants rear specialized, gongylidia-producing cultivars that lost their free-living relatives and could thus begin to co-evolve with the ants.
source: It was shown that: 1. the 'higher' attine ants to which the leaf-cutting ants belong rear specialized, gongylidia-producing cultivars that lost their free-living relatives and could thus begin to co-evolve with the ants (Schultz and Brady, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schultz and Brady, 2008.

claim: The leaf-cutting ant cultivar Leucocoprinus gongylophorus evolved to be obligatorily multinucleate and polyploid, which may well have allowed higher crop productivity.
source: 2. the leaf-cutting ant cultivar Leucocoprinus gongylophorus evolved to be obligatorily multinucleate and polyploid, which may well have allowed higher crop productivity (Kooij et al., 2015a)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kooij et al., 2015a, with speculation about the functional consequence.

claim: Leaf-cutting ant queens evolved to be multiply inseminated, in contrast to all phylogenetically more basal attines studied.
source: 3. leaf-cutting ant queens evolved to be multiply inseminated, in contrast to all phylogenetically more basal attines studied; this meant that not only the garden symbiont but also the farming ant families became genetically 'chimeric', albeit not as cell-lines but as lines of fungal nuclei and individual patrilines of ants (Villesen et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Villesen et al., 2002.

claim: Multiple insemination meant that both the garden symbiont and the farming ant families became genetically 'chimeric'.
source: 3. leaf-cutting ant queens evolved to be multiply inseminated, in contrast to all phylogenetically more basal attines studied; this meant that not only the garden symbiont but also the farming ant families became genetically 'chimeric', albeit not as cell-lines but as lines of fungal nuclei and individual patrilines of ants (Villesen et al., 2002)
evidence: This is an inference based on the multiple insemination finding cited to Villesen et al., 2002.

claim: The leaf-cutting ants evolved distinct division of labor within the worker caste, with small, medium, and large workers and specialized soldiers (the latter only in Atta).
source: 4. the leaf-cutting ants evolved distinct division of labor within the worker caste, with small, medium, and large workers and specialized soldiers (the latter only in Atta) (Weber, 1966)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Weber, 1966.

claim: The crown group of the attine ants underwent significant changes in their gut microbiota that likely facilitated the conversion efficiency of fungal diet substrate into ant biomass.
source: 5. the crown group of the attine ants underwent significant changes in their gut microbiota that likely facilitated the conversion efficiency of fungal diet substrate into ant biomass (Sapountzis et al., 2015; Sapountzis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sapountzis et al., 2015; Sapountzis et al., 2019.

claim: Cultivars likely changed their chitinase processing abilities in co-evolution with the ants' labial glands.
source: Recent genome sequencing showed that cultivars likely changed their chitinase processing abilities in co-evolution with the ants' labial glands (Nygaard et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nygaard et al., 2016.

claim: Proteases in the fecal fluid of Atta leaf-cutting ants had been produced by the fungal symbiont and passed unharmed through the ant guts to mediate protein degradation of the plant forage material.
source: These insights were initiated by pioneering work by Michael M. Martin (Boyd and Martin, 1975b; Boyd and Martin, 1975a; Martin and Martin, 1971; Martin and Martin, 1971), which suggested that proteases in the fecal fluid of Atta leaf-cutting ants had actually been produced by the fungal symbiont and passed unharmed through the ant guts to mediate protein degradation of the plant forage material when it was mixed with fecal fluid.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boyd and Martin, 1975b; Boyd and Martin, 1975a; Martin and Martin, 1971.

claim: The hypothesis that fungal proteases pass through ant guts unharmed was confirmed for Acromyrmex leaf-cutting ants.
source: Our previous work not only confirmed this hypothesis for Acromyrmex leaf-cutting ants (Kooij et al., 2014b)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kooij et al., 2014b.

claim: The list of cultivar-derived fecal fluid proteins was expanded to include pectinases, hemicellulases, and laccases.
source: but also expanded the list of cultivar-derived fecal fluid proteins to include pectinases, hemicellulases, and laccases (Rønhede et al., 2004; Schiøtt et al., 2010; De Fine Licht et al., 2013; Kooij et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rønhede et al., 2004; Schiøtt et al., 2010; De Fine Licht et al., 2013; Kooij et al., 2016.

claim: All fecal fluid enzymes are produced in the specialized gongylidia of the fungal cultivar that the ants ingest as their almost exclusive food source.
source: These studies also showed that all these enzymes are produced in the specialized gongylidia of the fungal cultivar that the ants ingest as their almost exclusive food source (Schiøtt et al., 2010; De Fine Licht et al., 2013; Kooij et al., 2014b; Kooij et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schiøtt et al., 2010; De Fine Licht et al., 2013; Kooij et al., 2014b; Kooij et al., 2016.

claim: Ant-produced pellets of chewed leaf material deposited on top of the garden turn black within a few hours.
source: First, the degradation of leaf fragments in Acromyrmex fungus gardens proceeds very efficiently, as ant-produced pellets of chewed leaf material deposited on top of the garden turn black within a few hours to then be spread out over the garden by the ants.
evidence: This is an observation of the behavior and appearance of substrate pellets.

claim: The fungal cultivar has lost a major ligninase domain.
source: Second, the fungal cultivar has lost a major ligninase domain (Nygaard et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nygaard et al., 2016.

claim: The proteomic analysis of worker fecal fluid from four different A. echinatior colonies identified 174 proteins.
source: Our proteomic analysis of worker fecal fluid from four different A. echinatior colonies identified 174 proteins (Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is a direct result from the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: 101 proteins were present in at least three of the four colony samples and constitute the core proteome.
source: To avoid including spurious proteins, we restricted our analyses to a shortlist of 101 proteins present in at least three of the four colony samples
evidence: This is based on the overlap analysis of the proteome data across colonies.

claim: 91 (90%) of the 101 core proteome proteins were able to be annotated.
source: and we were able to annotate 91 (90%) of these proteins (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on the annotation analysis of the identified proteins.

claim: The core proteome consisted mainly of degradation enzymes belonging to five major functional categories: oxidoreductases, proteolytic enzymes, carbohydrate active enzymes (CAZymes), phosphate-liberating enzymes, and lipid degrading enzymes.
source: This core proteome consisted mainly of degradation enzymes belonging to five major functional categories: oxidoreductases, proteolytic enzymes, carbohydrate active enzymes (CAZymes), phosphate-liberating enzymes, and lipid degrading enzymes (lipidolytic enzymes) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on the functional annotation of the proteome and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 86 of the core fecal proteome proteins originated from the fungal symbiont, with only 15 being encoded by the ant genome.
source: The vast majority (86) of the core fecal proteome originated from the fungal symbiont, with only 15 being encoded by the ant genome.
evidence: This is based on the origin analysis of the identified proteins.

claim: Alkaline phosphatase (Protein ID 75) and Laccase LgLcc1 (Protein ID 97) jointly made up almost a quarter of the total fecal protein mass.
source: Two specific proteins stood out as being exceptionally abundant (Supplementary file 1), the Alkaline phosphatase (Protein ID 75 in Table 1) and the previously described Laccase LgLcc1 (Protein ID 97 in Table 1; De Fine Licht et al., 2013), which jointly made up almost a quarter of the total fecal protein mass.
evidence: This is based on the LFQ intensity measurements from the proteome analysis.

claim: The five most abundant proteins contributed more than 40% of the total fecal protein mass.
source: Three other proteins also showed remarkably high LFQ-abundance levels: a 1,3-beta-glucanase (Protein ID 88 in Table 1), a Metallopeptidase M35 (Protein ID 206 in Table 1), and a Serine protease S53 (Protein ID 64 in Table 1), which implies that the five most abundant proteins contributed more than 40% of the total fecal protein mass.
evidence: This is based on the LFQ intensity measurements from the proteome analysis.

claim: Five of the identified oxidoreductases were annotated as fungal glucose-methanol-choline (GMC) oxidoreductases.
source: Five of the identified oxidoreductases were annotated as fungal glucose-methanol-choline (GMC) oxidoreductases.
evidence: This is based on the annotation of the proteome data.

claim: A subgroup of GMC oxidoreductases are the aryl alcohol oxidases that are believed to play an important role in lignin degradation by brown-rot fungi.
source: A subgroup of these enzymes are the aryl alcohol oxidases that are believed to play an important role in lignin degradation by brown-rot fungi (Guillén et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Guillén et al., 2000.

claim: Brown-rot fungi are distinct from white-rot fungi, which degrade lignin using ligninolytic peroxidases.
source: This category of wood degrading fungi is distinct from the white-rot fungi, which degrade lignin using ligninolytic peroxidases (Arantes et al., 2012; Arantes and Goodell, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arantes et al., 2012; Arantes and Goodell, 2014.

claim: The ligninolytic peroxidase mechanism has most likely evolved only once in the Agaricomycotina lineage but has subsequently been lost many times giving a complex phylogenetic pattern.
source: The latter mechanism has most likely evolved only once in the Agaricomycotina lineage (to which Leucocoprinus belongs), but has subsequently been lost many times giving a complex phylogenetic pattern (Floudas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Floudas et al., 2012.

claim: The leaf-cutting ant cultivar has lost its ligninolytic peroxidases.
source: We showed previously (Nygaard et al., 2016) that the leaf-cutting ant cultivar has lost its ligninolytic peroxidases
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nygaard et al., 2016.

claim: Brown-rot fungi produce aromatic alcohols, which are subsequently oxidized by aryl alcohol oxidases to produce hydrogen peroxide.
source: In order to break down lignocellulose, brown-rot fungi produce aromatic alcohols, which are subsequently oxidized by aryl alcohol oxidases to produce hydrogen peroxide (H2O2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about brown-rot fungi biochemistry.

claim: In the Fenton reaction, hydrogen peroxide reacts with reduced iron (Fe2+) to produce hydroxyl radicals that can diffuse into the lignocellulose substrate and break chemical bonds.
source: The hydrogen peroxide is subsequently used in a Fenton reaction in which reduced iron (Fe2+) reacts with hydrogen peroxide to produce hydroxyl radicals that can diffuse into the lignocellulose substrate and break the chemical bonds responsible for the rigid structure of lignocellulose.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Fenton reaction mechanism.

claim: It has been suggested that fungi secrete secondary metabolites such as hydroquinones to reduce Fe3+ to Fe2+.
source: It has therefore been suggested that fungi secrete secondary metabolites such as hydroquinones to reduce Fe3+ to Fe2+ (Suzuki et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Suzuki et al., 2006.

claim: Acromyrmex colonies concentrate their chewed leaf fragments in pellets of ca. 3 mm diameter at the top of their fungus gardens for some hours before the material is dispersed.
source: As it appears, the spatial issue appears to have been resolved because Acromyrmex colonies concentrate their chewed leaf fragments in pellets of ca. 3 mm diameter at the top of their fungus gardens for some hours before the material is dispersed across the actively growing ridges of the fungal mycelium mass.
evidence: This is an observation of ant behavior in the fungus garden.

claim: Glucose dehydrogenase (Protein ID 145) is the most abundant ant-encoded fecal fluid protein.
source: We hypothesized that glucose dehydrogenase (Protein ID 145 in Table 1), the most abundant ant-encoded fecal fluid protein (Table 1, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is based on the LFQ intensity measurements from the proteome analysis.

claim: All five fungal GMC oxidoreductases isolated from fecal fluid clustered within the aryl alcohol oxidases in a phylogenetic tree.
source: A phylogenetic tree of all five fungal GMC oxidoreductases isolated from fecal fluid, together with representative GMC oxidoreductases from various basidiomycete fungi, showed that these five enzymes clustered within the aryl alcohol oxidases (Figure 3)
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Fecal fluid contained a substantial amount of hydrogen peroxide.
source: We subsequently measured the amount of hydrogen peroxide that these GMC oxidoreductases produce with and without substrates, which showed that fecal fluid contained a substantial amount of hydrogen peroxide.
evidence: This is based on the hydrogen peroxide measurement assay.

claim: Addition of aromatic veratryl alcohol increased the amount of hydrogen peroxide in fecal fluid, whereas glucose and methanol did not have any effect.
source: Addition of aromatic veratryl alcohol further increased this amount, whereas glucose and methanol did not have any effect (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is based on the hydrogen peroxide measurement assay shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Catalase completely removed the hydrogen peroxide signal, confirming that hydrogen peroxide is indeed naturally produced in fecal fluid.
source: As expected, catalase completely removed the signal, confirming that hydrogen peroxide is indeed naturally produced in fecal fluid (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on the hydrogen peroxide measurement assay with catalase control shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Two fecal fluid oxidoreductases (Protein IDs 81 and 186) were annotated as copper radical oxidases with close similarity to glyoxal oxidases.
source: Two other fecal fluid oxidoreductases (Protein IDs 81 and 186 in Table 1) were annotated as copper radical oxidases with close similarity to glyoxal oxidases.
evidence: This is based on the annotation of the proteome data.

claim: Glyoxal oxidases may produce hydrogen peroxide, using the small organic compound glyoxal and other aldehydes as substrate.
source: These enzymes may also produce hydrogen peroxide, using the small organic compound glyoxal and other aldehydes as substrate (Daou and Faulds, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Daou and Faulds, 2017.

claim: Experimental addition of glyoxal to fecal fluid of Acromyrmex worker increased the amount of hydrogen peroxide, confirming that glyoxal oxidases are present in the fecal fluid.
source: Experimental addition of glyoxal to fecal fluid of Acromyrmex worker did indeed increase the amount of hydrogen peroxide, confirming that glyoxal oxidases are also present in the fecal fluid (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on the hydrogen peroxide measurement assay with glyoxal shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The average iron level in fecal fluid across six ant colonies was 370 ± 110 µM.
source: We measured the iron levels in fecal fluid and found an average (± SD) level of 370 ± 110 µM iron across six ant colonies.
evidence: This is based on the iron level measurement assay.

claim: The concentration of iron in fecal fluid should be sufficient to allow the Fenton reaction to occur.
source: This concentration of iron should be sufficient to allow the Fenton reaction to occur (Hegnar et al., 2019; Elias and Waterhouse, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hegnar et al., 2019; Elias and Waterhouse, 2010.

claim: The iron concentration in fecal fluid corresponds to the levels relevant for natural wood degrading systems.
source: It corresponds to the levels relevant for natural wood degrading systems (Hegnar et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hegnar et al., 2019.

claim: The iron concentration in fecal fluid is one to two orders of magnitude lower than the levels typically used for pretreatment of plant biomass in vitro.
source: although it is one to two orders of magnitude lower than the levels typically used for pretreatment of plant biomass in vitro (Jung et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jung et al., 2015.

claim: Pronounced amounts of hydroxyl radicals were present in the ant fecal fluid as measured by the 2-deoxy-D-ribose assay.
source: To quantify this effect, we adapted the standard 2-deoxy-D-ribose assay to accommodate the small volumes of fecal fluid that could practically be collected directly from the ants and found pronounced amounts of hydroxyl radicals to be present in the ant fecal fluid (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on the deoxyribose assay shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Adding 1,10-phenanthroline caused a significant reduction in absorbance in the deoxyribose assay, consistent with hydroxyl radicals being produced by Fenton chemistry.
source: Adding a strong metal chelator 1,10-phenanthroline caused a significant reduction in absorbance. This is consistent with the hydroxyl radicals being produced by Fenton chemistry because the Fenton reaction is known to be inhibited by 1,10-phenanthroline's strong iron sequestering activity (Winterbourn, 1995).
evidence: This is based on the deoxyribose assay with phenanthroline, supported by citation to Winterbourn, 1995.

claim: The phenanthroline effect was not observed when only the solvent of the 1,10-phenanthroline chemical (methanol) was added.
source: This effect was not observed when only the solvent of the 1,10-phenanthroline chemical (methanol) was added.
evidence: This is based on the control experiment in the deoxyribose assay.

claim: A measurable capacity for Fe3+ reduction was found in fecal fluid.
source: We indeed found a measurable capacity for Fe3+ reduction in fecal fluid
evidence: This is based on the Ferrozine assay.

claim: The capacity for Fe3+ reduction in fecal fluid was increased by the addition of glucose.
source: which was further increased by the addition of glucose. This was consistent with Fe3+ being actively recycled into Fe2+ via fecal fluid compounds and with glucose dehydrogenase most likely being responsible for at least part of this activity (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on the Ferrozine assay shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Preliminary experiments using laccase substrates did not change the rate of Fe3+ reduction.
source: Preliminary experiments using laccase substrates in these assays did, however, not change the rate of Fe3+ reduction.
evidence: This is based on preliminary experimental results.

claim: The presence of fungal enzymes in the fecal fluid of leaf-cutting ants was suggested in the 1970s based on the biochemical similarity of proteases in fecal fluid and the fungal cultivar.
source: The presence of fungal enzymes in the fecal fluid of leaf-cutting ants was suggested already in the 1970s based on the biochemical similarity of proteases in fecal fluid and the fungal cultivar (Boyd and Martin, 1975b; Boyd and Martin, 1975a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boyd and Martin, 1975b; Boyd and Martin, 1975a.

claim: When run on SDS-Page gels, the fecal fluid proteins always gave the same banding pattern.
source: When run on SDS-Page gels (Schiøtt et al., 2010), the fecal fluid proteins always gave the same banding pattern
evidence: This is based on experimental observation cited to Schiøtt et al., 2010.

claim: The consistent banding pattern rejects the null hypothesis that fecal fluid proteins are a random collection of proteins that happen to escape digestion.
source: rejecting the null hypothesis that they are a random collection of proteins that happen to escape digestion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistent banding pattern observation.

claim: Alkaline phosphatase (Protein ID 75) had the highest abundance of all fecal proteins.
source: That alkaline phosphatase (Protein ID 75 in Table 1) had the highest abundance of all fecal proteins underlines the importance of phosphorus mineralization.
evidence: This is based on the LFQ intensity measurements from the proteome analysis.

claim: The high abundance of alkaline phosphatase underlines the importance of phosphorus mineralization.
source: That alkaline phosphatase (Protein ID 75 in Table 1) had the highest abundance of all fecal proteins underlines the importance of phosphorus mineralization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high abundance of alkaline phosphatase.

claim: Phytin is a phosphorus-storage compound in plant seeds, but also occurs in pollen and vegetative tissues.
source: Phytin is a phosphorus-storage compound in plant seeds, but also occurs in pollen and vegetative tissues (Brinch-Pedersen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brinch-Pedersen et al., 2002.

claim: In nature leaf-cutting ants are not known to forage on seeds to any significant degree.
source: but in nature leaf-cutting ants are not known to forage on seeds to any significant degree (Kooij et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kooij et al., 2014a.

claim: Leaf-cutting ants do harvest flowers, whose pollen may be a source of phytin.
source: However, they do harvest flowers, whose pollen may be a source of phytin.
evidence: This is an inference based on known ant behavior and the presence of phytin in pollen.

claim: The fecal lipidolytic enzymes had low abundances overall.
source: The fecal lipidolytic enzymes had low abundances overall.
evidence: This is based on the LFQ intensity measurements from the proteome analysis.

claim: Lipidolytic enzymes may play a function in degrading cell membranes to liberate cytosolic compounds as has been shown for biotrophic fungi.
source: Apart from digesting lipids into assimilatory products, these enzymes may also hplay a function in degrading cell membranes to liberate cytosolic compounds as has been shown for biotrophic fungi (Ghannoum, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ghannoum, 2000.

claim: Lipidolytic enzymes may interfere with signal transduction pathways involved in plant resistance toward pathogens.
source: They may also interfere with signal transduction pathways involved in plant resistance toward pathogens (Wu and Li, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wu and Li, 2015.

claim: Brown-rot fungi are believed to have a reduced array of enzymes targeting lignocellulose compared to white-rot fungi, and to specifically lack lignin peroxidases.
source: Compared to white-rot fungi, brown-rot fungi are believed to have a reduced array of enzymes targeting lignocellulose, and to specifically lack lignin peroxidases, which is also the case for L. gongylophorus (Nygaard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about brown-rot fungi, with citation to Nygaard et al., 2016 for L. gongylophorus.

claim: Brown-rot fungi compensate their lack of enzymatic potential by using Fenton chemistry to degrade lignocellulose while producing extracellular hydroxyl radicals.
source: Brown-rot fungi compensate this lack of enzymatic potential by using Fenton chemistry to degrade lignocellulose while producing extracellular hydroxyl radicals (Arantes and Goodell, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arantes and Goodell, 2014.

claim: In the Fenton reaction, hydrogen peroxide reacts with ferrous iron (Fe2+) and hydrogen ions to produce ferric iron (Fe3+), water, and hydroxyl radicals.
source: In the Fenton reaction, hydrogen peroxide reacts with ferrous iron (Fe2+) and hydrogen ions to produce ferric iron (Fe3+), water, and hydroxyl radicals (Guillén et al., 2000; Arantes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guillén et al., 2000; Arantes et al., 2012.

claim: Hydroxyl radicals produced in brown-rot fungi are known to damage a wide range of biomolecules.
source: The very reactive hydroxyl radicals produced in these free-living fungi are known to damage a wide range of biomolecules (Halliwell et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Halliwell et al., 1988.

claim: Hydroxyl radicals release soluble carbohydrate fragments from plant cell walls.
source: Their putative functions are: 1. to release soluble carbohydrate fragments from plant cell walls (Schweikert et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schweikert et al., 2002.

claim: Hydroxyl radicals reduce the viscosity of solutions containing plant cell wall components such as xyloglucan, pectin, and cellulose.
source: and 2. to reduce the viscosity of solutions containing plant cell wall components such as xyloglucan, pectin, and cellulose (Fry, 1998)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fry, 1998.

claim: The small size of hydroxyl radical molecules allows them to initiate penetration and cleavage of lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose polymers in preparation for further degradation into assimilatory monomers by specific enzymes.
source: The small size of hydroxyl radical molecules allows them to initiate penetration and cleavage of lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose polymers in preparation for further degradation into assimilatory monomers by specific enzymes (Arantes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arantes et al., 2012.

claim: Brown-rot fungi are believed to use GMC oxidoreductases or copper radical oxidases to aerobically oxidize fungal alcohols or aldehydes in order to produce hydrogen peroxide.
source: Brown-rot fungi are believed to use GMC oxidoreductases or copper radical oxidases to aerobically oxidize fungal alcohols or aldehydes in order to produce hydrogen peroxide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about brown-rot fungi biochemistry.

claim: Brown-rot fungi obtain the required iron from the wood substrate or via active mycelial transport into the degrading wood.
source: In this process they then obtain the required iron from the wood substrate (Arantes et al., 2012) or via actively mycelial transport into the degrading wood (Kirker et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arantes et al., 2012 and Kirker et al., 2017.

claim: It has been suggested that fungal laccases oxidize hydroquinones into semiquinones that react with ferric iron (Fe3+) to produce quinones and ferrous iron (Fe2+).
source: It has been suggested that fungal laccases are then oxidizing hydroquinones into the semiquinones that react with ferric iron (Fe3+) to produce quinones and ferrous iron (Fe2+), which would produce the recycling process needed to maintain the Fenton reaction over time (Guillén et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Guillén et al., 2000.

claim: The details of Fenton chemistry in brown-rot fungi have remained rather little known in spite of the economic importance of these fungi.
source: It is intriguing that the details of Fenton chemistry in brown-rot fungi have remained rather little known in spite of the economic importance of these fungi (Arantes and Goodell, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arantes and Goodell, 2014.

claim: The leaf-cutting ants offered an unexpected window for understanding the elusive Fenton process in brown-rot fungi.
source: and that the leaf-cutting ants offered an unexpected window for understanding this elusive process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: The identified GMC oxidoreductases were aryl alcohol oxidases, which are known to produce hydrogen peroxide from aromatic alcohols.
source: We could verify that the identified GMC oxidoreductases were aryl alcohol oxidases (Figure 3), which are known to produce hydrogen peroxide from aromatic alcohols.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3 and established knowledge.

claim: Fecal fluid contains concentrated hydrogen peroxide and the concentration increased further after adding veratryl alcohol or glyoxal.
source: We also verified that fecal fluid contains concentrated hydrogen peroxide and that the concentration increased further after adding veratryl alcohol or glyoxal, which are substrates for GMC oxidoreductases and copper radical oxidases, respectively (Guillén et al., 1992; Daou and Faulds, 2017).
evidence: This is based on the hydrogen peroxide assay, supported by citations to Guillén et al., 1992; Daou and Faulds, 2017.

claim: The iron content of the fecal fluid is maintained at levels that are amply permissive for Fenton chemistry to occur.
source: We further documented that the iron content of the fecal fluid is maintained at levels that are amply permissive for Fenton chemistry to occur.
evidence: This is based on the iron level measurement assay.

claim: The acid pH of ca. 4 in the fecal fluid should be ideal for Fenton chemistry.
source: Also the acid pH of ca. 4 in the fecal fluid should be ideal for Fenton chemistry (Bishop et al., 1968; Erthal et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bishop et al., 1968; Erthal et al., 2004.

claim: Fecal fluid components degrade deoxyribose into thiobarbituric acid-active products, which can only be explained by the presence of hydroxyl radicals.
source: Finally, a separate assay showed that fecal fluid components degrade deoxyribose into thiobarbituric acid-active products, which can only be explained by the presence of hydroxyl radicals (Halliwell et al., 1988).
evidence: This is based on the deoxyribose assay, supported by citation to Halliwell et al., 1988.

claim: Brown-rot fungi are widely believed to use hydroxyl radicals for substrate degradation.
source: whereas brown-rot fungi are widely believed to use hydroxyl radicals for substrate degradation (Arantes and Goodell, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arantes and Goodell, 2014.

claim: Specialized functions of the ant fecal fluid aimed at plant substrate degradation are uncontroversial.
source: We also note that specialized functions of the ant fecal fluid aimed at plant substrate degradation are uncontroversial (Boyd and Martin, 1975b; Boyd and Martin, 1975a; Martin and Martin, 1971; Kooij et al., 2014b; Rønhede et al., 2004; Schiøtt et al., 2010; De Fine Licht et al., 2013; Kooij et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The high concentrations of laccase LgLcc1 (Protein ID 97) in the ant fecal fluid suggest a similar mechanism for maintaining reliable conversion of Fe3+ back to Fe2+ as the Fenton chemistry known from brown-rot fungi.
source: The high concentrations of laccase LgLcc1 (Protein ID 97 in Table 1) in the ant fecal fluid suggest a similar mechanism for maintaining reliable conversion of Fe3+ back to Fe2+ (using hydroquinone as an electron donor) as the Fenton chemistry known from brown-rot fungi (Guillén et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an inference based on the high laccase abundance and known mechanisms in brown-rot fungi, supported by citation to Guillén et al., 2000.

claim: The glucose dehydrogenase (Protein ID 145) encoded by the ant genome was abundant in the fecal proteome and could convert Fe3+ back to Fe2+ via simultaneous oxidization of glucose.
source: However, the glucose dehydrogenase (Protein ID 145 in Table 1) encoded by the ant genome was also abundant in the fecal proteome and could convert Fe3+ back to Fe2+ via simultaneous oxidization of glucose.
evidence: This is based on the proteome data and the Ferrozine assay.

claim: The Ferrozine-based assay verified that glucose dehydrogenase can convert Fe3+ back to Fe2+ and that this function is dependent on glucose availability.
source: We verified this putative function as likely with a Ferrozine-based assay (Goodell et al., 2006), including its dependence on glucose availability.
evidence: This is based on the Ferrozine assay, supported by citation to Goodell et al., 2006.

claim: Adding laccase substrates did not influence the velocity of the Fe3+ to Fe2+ reduction reaction.
source: Interestingly, however, preliminary experiments indicated that adding laccase substrates did not influence the velocity of this reaction
evidence: This is based on preliminary experimental results.

claim: Glucose liberated from the plant polysaccharides is primarily used to keep the Fenton reaction going.
source: which suggests that glucose liberated from the plant polysaccharides is primarily used to keep the Fenton reaction going.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of laccase substrates on Fe3+ reduction.

claim: The glucose dependence of Fe3+ reduction may provide an additional feedback loop for the farming symbiotic partnership to control the inorganic Fenton chemistry process.
source: This substrate dependence may provide an additional feedback loop for the farming symbiotic partnership to control the inorganic Fenton chemistry process.
evidence: This is speculation based on the glucose-dependent Fe3+ reduction.

claim: The ant-derived glucose dehydrogenase alternative might allow the ants to use the fungal laccases specifically for the decomposition of secondary plant compounds.
source: The ant-derived glucose dehydrogenase (Protein ID 145 in Table 1) alternative might allow the ants to also use the fungal laccases specifically for the decomposition of secondary plant compounds as found in one of our previous studies (De Fine Licht et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to De Fine Licht et al., 2013.

claim: LgLcc1 (Protein ID 97) came under positive selection in the common ancestor of the leaf-cutting ants.
source: That study also suggested that LgLcc1 (Protein ID 97 in Table 1) came under positive selection in the common ancestor of the leaf-cutting ants
evidence: This is based on a previous study's findings.

claim: Positive selection on LgLcc1 would be consistent with laccase becoming redundant for iron reduction and therefore undergoing directional selection for other functions.
source: which would be consistent with laccase becoming redundant for iron reduction and therefore undergoing directional selection for other functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the positive selection finding.

claim: The assembly of complementary components from different sources implies that the fungal cultivar and the farming ants synergistically cooperate to accomplish the continued production of hydroxyl radicals.
source: The assembly of complementary components from different sources implies that the fungal cultivar and the farming ants synergistically cooperate to accomplish the continued production of hydroxyl radicals, but only as long as Fenton chemistry is needed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteome findings showing components from both ant and fungus.

claim: The ants do not appear to keep adding fecal fluid to existing Fenton pellets.
source: The ants do not appear to keep adding fecal fluid to existing Fenton pellets
evidence: This is an observation of ant behavior.

claim: Ants take Fenton pellets apart when they have turned black after some hours to distribute the Fenton exposed leaf fragments over the actively growing ridges of the fungus garden.
source: and they take them apart when they have turned black after some hours to distribute the Fenton exposed leaf fragments over the actively growing ridges of the fungus garden where fungal decomposition takes over.
evidence: This is an observation of ant behavior.

claim: Both the processing efficiency and the ultimate behavioral control by the ants strongly suggest refined co-adaptation at the molecular level to enable colonies to operate as integrated functional herbivores.
source: Both the processing efficiency and the ultimate behavioral control by the ants strongly suggest refined co-adaptation at the molecular level to enable colonies to operate as integrated functional herbivores.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed efficiency and behavioral control.

claim: An earlier study found a high expression of an NADH-quinone oxidoreductase in fungus gardens of A. echinatior.
source: An earlier study found a high expression of an NADH-quinone oxidoreductase in fungus gardens of A. echinatior (Grell et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grell et al., 2013.

claim: NADH-quinone oxidoreductase is an enzyme converting quinones to hydroquinones that can react with Fe3+ to form Fe2+ after conversion to semiquinones by laccase.
source: an enzyme converting quinones to hydroquinones that can react with Fe3+ to form Fe2+ after conversion to semiquinones by laccase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the enzyme's function.

claim: The presence of NADH-quinone oxidoreductase is consistent with the ant encoded glucose dehydrogenase being relevant only for the degradation process in the Fenton pellets.
source: This is consistent with the ant encoded glucose dehydrogenase being relevant only for the degradation process in the Fenton pellets
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of NADH-quinone oxidoreductase in the fungus garden.

claim: NADH-quinone oxidoreductases take over iron reduction after the leaf fragments have been dispersed over the garden and the fungal hyphae decompose what remains of the substrate.
source: and with NADH-quinone oxidoreductases taking over after the leaf fragments have been dispersed over the garden and the fungal hyphae decompose what remains of the substrate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of NADH-quinone oxidoreductase in the fungus garden.

claim: Aryl alcohol oxidases use aromatic alcohols as a substrate to produce hydrogen peroxide.
source: Aryl alcohol oxidases use aromatic alcohols as a substrate to produce hydrogen peroxide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about aryl alcohol oxidases.

claim: White-rot fungi produce aromatic veratryl alcohol as a secondary metabolite, which plays several important roles for ligninolysis.
source: White-rot fungi produce aromatic veratryl alcohol as a secondary metabolite, which plays several important roles for ligninolysis (Jensen et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jensen et al., 1994.

claim: Veratryl alcohol is derived from phenylalanine via the phenylalanine/tyrosine pathway that has previously been shown to be upregulated in the gongylidia of the A. echinatior cultivar L. gongylophorus.
source: Veratryl alcohol is derived from phenylalanine via the phenylalanine/tyrosine pathway that has previously been shown to be upregulated in the gongylidia of the A. echinatior cultivar L. gongylophorus (De Fine Licht et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to De Fine Licht et al., 2014.

claim: Veratryl alcohol (or a derivative thereof) may be produced in the gongylidia of the fungal cultivar to be ingested but not digested by the ants so it can function in the fecal fluid to facilitate the initial stages of substrate degradation.
source: This might suggest that veratryl alcohol (or a derivative thereof) is produced in the gongylidia of the fungal cultivar to be ingested but not digested by the ants so it can function in the fecal fluid to facilitate the initial stages of substrate degradation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the upregulation of the phenylalanine/tyrosine pathway in gongylidia.

claim: The hydrogen peroxide needed in the Fenton reaction may be derived from the activity of the glyoxal oxidases.
source: The hydrogen peroxide needed in the Fenton reaction may also be derived from the activity of the glyoxal oxidases that we identified, which use various aldehydes as substrate for hydrogen peroxide production (Daou and Faulds, 2017).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Daou and Faulds, 2017.

claim: Aldehydes used by glyoxal oxidases could either originate from the oxidized aryl alcohols produced by the aryl alcohol oxidases, or could be direct degradation products from plant cell wall components.
source: Such aldehydes could then either originate from the oxidized aryl alcohols produced by the aryl alcohol oxidases, or could be direct degradation products from plant cell wall components (Daou and Faulds, 2017).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Daou and Faulds, 2017.

claim: Multiple parallel pathways suggest that the co-evolved interactions between inorganic Fenton chemistry and organic enzyme functions are likely to have robust operational functionality under a variety of environmental conditions.
source: These multiple parallel pathways suggest that the co-evolved interactions between inorganic Fenton chemistry and organic enzyme functions are likely to have robust operational functionality under a variety of environmental (i.e. substrate) conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of multiple pathways.

claim: Hydroxyl radicals are highly toxic also for the organisms producing them.
source: Finally, as we explained in the introduction, it is important to note that hydroxyl radicals are highly toxic also for the organisms producing them.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hydroxyl radicals.

claim: The toxicity of hydroxyl radicals probably constrains the use of naturally produced hydroxyl radicals for biomass degradation unless the Fenton chemistry remains distal to hyphal growth and is terminated by the time hyphae grow into the substrate patches.
source: This probably constrains the use of naturally produced hydroxyl radicals for biomass degradation unless the Fenton chemistry producing these radicals remains distal to hyphal growth and is terminated by the time hyphae grow into the substrate patches pre-treated in this manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the toxicity of hydroxyl radicals.

claim: The constraint of hydroxyl radical toxicity will slow down the rate of decomposition in free-living fungi.
source: This complication will slow down the rate of decomposition in free-living fungi
evidence: This is an inference based on the toxicity constraint.

claim: The leaf-cutting ant symbiotic partnership appears to have resolved the hydroxyl radical toxicity constraint by compartmentalizing the complementary elements of initial aggressive break down of plant substrate.
source: but the leaf-cutting ant symbiotic partnership appears to have resolved this constraint by compartmentalizing the complementary elements of initial aggressive break down of plant substrate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed spatial separation of Fenton chemistry in pellets.

claim: Although the necessary compounds for the Fenton reaction are all present in the guts of the ants, the low oxygen pressure there would presumably prevent the production of hydrogen peroxide inside the ants.
source: Although the necessary compounds for the Fenton reaction are all present in the guts of the ants, the low oxygen pressure there would presumably prevent the production of hydrogen peroxide inside the ants and thereby any collateral damage to ant tissues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known low oxygen environment in insect guts.

claim: Defecation onto concentrated pellets of chewed leaf fragments ensures that the Fenton reaction does not start until atmospheric oxygen is available.
source: Defecation onto concentrated pellets of chewed leaf fragments thus ensures that the reaction does not start until atmospheric oxygen is available.
evidence: This is an inference based on the oxygen requirement for hydrogen peroxide production.

claim: The Fenton pellets appear to function as small bioconversion reactors that are spatially isolated from both the fungal and the ant tissues so that potentially harmful side-effects are avoided.
source: Consequently, the Fenton pellets appear to function as small bioconversion reactors that are spatially isolated from both the fungal and the ant tissues so that potentially harmful side-effects are avoided.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial separation of Fenton chemistry.

claim: A. echinatior has more glutathione S-transferase genes than other (non-attine) ants, despite having fewer detoxification genes in general.
source: Our recent genome sequencing study of Acromyrmex ants and their cultivars revealed that A. echinatior has more glutathione S-transferase genes than other (non-attine) ants, despite having fewer detoxification genes in general (Nygaard et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nygaard et al., 2011.

claim: Glutathione S-transferase is known to be involved in the breakdown of oxidized lipids.
source: Glutathione S-transferase is known to be involved in the breakdown of oxidized lipids
evidence: This is established knowledge about glutathione S-transferase function.

claim: The presence of more glutathione S-transferase genes suggests that physiological mechanisms to ameliorate inadvertent damage caused by hydroxyl radicals may be in place, should they appear in the ant gut before the excretion of fecal fluid.
source: This suggests that physiological mechanisms to ameliorate inadvertent damage caused by hydroxyl radicals may be in place, should they appear in the ant gut before the excretion of fecal fluid.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased number of glutathione S-transferase genes.

claim: The extent to which cellulose is degraded in the fungus garden has been widely disputed.
source: The extent to which cellulose is degraded in the fungus garden has been widely disputed (see Grell et al., 2013 and references therein).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grell et al., 2013.

claim: The fecal fluid proteome only contained a single 1,4-beta-glucanase (Protein ID 55) to target the cellulose backbone, and this protein was found in low quantities and in only three of the four examined colonies.
source: It is noteworthy that the fecal fluid proteome only contained a single 1,4-beta-glucanase (Protein ID 55 in Table 1) to target the cellulose backbone, and that this protein was found in low quantities and in only three of the four examined colonies.
evidence: This is based on the proteome analysis.

claim: A single 1,4-beta-glucosidase (Protein ID 73) that releases glucose moieties from cellobiose and oligosaccharides was found, but this enzyme is also targeting hemicellulose in addition to cellulose.
source: We also found a single 1,4-beta-glucosidase (Protein ID 73 in Table 1) that releases glucose moieties from cellobiose and oligosaccharides, but this enzyme is also targeting hemicellulose in addition to cellulose.
evidence: This is based on the proteome analysis and known enzyme function.

claim: Effective degradation of cellulose normally requires the enzyme cellobiohydrolase, which was only found in one colony in very low quantities.
source: Finally, effective degradation of cellulose normally requires the enzyme cellobiohydrolase, which was only found in one colony in very low quantities (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on the proteome analysis and known requirements for cellulose degradation.

claim: The findings are consistent with cellulose degradation not being a primary function of the fecal fluid.
source: These findings are consistent with our earlier inference (Grell et al., 2013; Moller et al., 2011) that cellulose degradation is not a primary function of the fecal fluid
evidence: This is an inference based on the low abundance of cellulose-degrading enzymes, supported by citations to Grell et al., 2013; Moller et al., 2011.

claim: Recalcitrant plant cell wall cellulose is not degraded to a significant degree in Acromyrmex fungus gardens, but discarded from the colony as waste.
source: supporting earlier findings that recalcitrant plant cell wall cellulose is not degraded to a significant degree in Acromyrmex fungus gardens, but discarded from the colony as waste (Moller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Moller et al., 2011.

claim: Fenton chemistry may be used for breaking chemical bonds in cell wall lignocellulose and is likely sufficient to give hyphal degradation enzymes access to their target substrates in the interior of plant cells.
source: Our finding that Fenton chemistry may be used for breaking chemical bonds in cell wall lignocellulose and is likely sufficient to give hyphal degradation enzymes access to their target substrates in the interior of plant cells, appears to corroborate this notion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Fenton chemistry findings.

claim: More complete cellulose degradation would release an excess of assimilatory sugars for the fungal symbiont but without simultaneously providing nitrogen or phosphorus, which are the limiting factors for growth in any functional herbivore.
source: More complete cellulose degradation would release an excess of assimilatory sugars for the fungal symbiont but without simultaneously providing nitrogen or phosphorus, which are the limiting factors for growth in any functional herbivore (Elser et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Elser et al., 2007.

claim: Excess sugars from complete cellulose degradation could be a burden for the symbiosis if they would allow inadvertent microorganisms to thrive in fungus gardens.
source: Such sugars could well be a burden for the symbiosis if they would allow inadvertent microorganisms to thrive in fungus gardens (Grell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Grell et al., 2013.

claim: Fenton pellets have never been observed in any of the Atta colonies maintained in the lab for ca. 25 years.
source: it is intriguing that we have never observed Fenton pellets in any of the Atta colonies that we have maintained in the lab for ca. 25 years.
evidence: This is an observation from long-term colony maintenance.

claim: The absence of Fenton pellets in Atta suggests that the colonies of this genus have evolved alternative mechanisms to boost the efficiency and robustness of their functional herbivory.
source: This suggests that the colonies of this other genus of leaf-cutting ants, which are approximately two orders of magnitude larger in size and considerably more damaging as agricultural pests have evolved alternative mechanisms to boost the efficiency and robustness of their functional herbivory.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of Fenton pellets in Atta.

claim: Both Acromyrmex and Atta colonies produce enormous amounts of cellulose rich waste.
source: Given that also Atta colonies produce enormous amounts of cellulose rich waste
evidence: This is an observation of colony waste production.

claim: Both Acromyrmex and Atta genera rear very closely related lineages of the L. gongylophorus cultivars in sympatry at the Panamanian sampling site and across their Latin American distributions.
source: This is because both genera rear very closely related lineages of the L. gongylophorus cultivars in sympatry at our Panamanian sampling site (Kooij et al., 2015b) and across their Latin American distributions (Silva-Pinhati et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kooij et al., 2015b and Silva-Pinhati et al., 2004.

claim: Human in vitro experiments with Fenton chemistry have produced up to fivefold increases in the production of sugars from feedstock, although the efficiency remains highly dependent on the plant material used.
source: Another point of interest is that human in vitro experiments with Fenton chemistry have produced up to fivefold increases in the production of sugars from feedstock, although the efficiency remains highly dependent on the plant material used (Kato et al., 2014; Jung et al., 2015; Hegnar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kato et al., 2014; Jung et al., 2015; Hegnar et al., 2019.

claim: A major challenge in human bioconversion applications has been that the Fenton generated reactive oxygen species degrade the very enzymes that are instrumental in maintaining sustainable conversion efficiency.
source: A major challenge in these human bioconversion applications has been that the Fenton generated reactive oxygen species degrade the very enzymes that are instrumental in maintaining sustainable conversion efficiency.
evidence: This is established knowledge about challenges in human bioconversion technology.

claim: Colonies of Acromyrmex echinatior were collected in Gamboa, Panama between 2001 and 2010.
source: Colonies of Acromyrmex echinatior (numbers Ae150, Ae160, Ae263, Ae322, Ae356, Ae372, Ae480, and Ae490) were collected in Gamboa, Panama between 2001 and 2010
evidence: This is a description of the biological material collection.

claim: Colonies were maintained in the laboratory at ca. 25°C and ca. 70% relative humidity.
source: and maintained in the laboratory at ca. 25°C and ca. 70% relative humidity (Bot and Boomsma, 1996)
evidence: This is a description of the colony maintenance conditions, supported by citation to Bot and Boomsma, 1996.

claim: Colonies were supplied with a diet of bramble leaves, occasional dry rice, and pieces of apple.
source: where they were supplied with a diet of bramble leaves, occasional dry rice, and pieces of apple.
evidence: This is a description of the colony diet.
